semi-log-plots-s1.title: Users of an app on a semi-log plot
semi-log-plots-s1.text: The vertical axis is a logarithmic scale. Points $A(0, 20)$, $B(4, 200)$ and $C(8, 2{,}000)$ lie on the line through the data, where $t$ is years since 2016.

table.caption: Values of t and of the common logarithm of y, from data plotted on a semi-log plot

items.q: The data lie on a straight line on this semi-log plot. What does that show about the number of users?
options: It grows exponentially, by the same factor in equal times
It grows linearly: equal time steps add the same number of users
It grows like a quadratic: its second differences are constant
It grows logarithmically: it rises by equal steps as $t$ doubles

why.correct: On a logarithmic vertical scale, equal vertical steps are equal factors. A straight line rises by equal steps over equal times, so the count is multiplied by the same factor each year: exponential growth.
options: Straight on a semi-log plot means $\log y$ is linear in $t$, so $y$ is exponential.
Linear data would bend (concave down) on a log scale, because equal additions are smaller and smaller factors.
A quadratic's logarithm is not linear in $t$, so it would not make a straight line.
Logarithmic growth would bend even more on a log scale.

items.q: From $A$ to $B$, how does the number of users change?
options: It is multiplied by $10$
It increases by $10$ users
It is multiplied by $4$
It is multiplied by $100$

why.correct: $B$ is one labeled step (one power of $10$) above $A$: from $20$ to $200$, a factor of $10$, over $4$ years.
options: The count goes from $20$ to $200$, up $180$; on a log scale, equal steps are factors, not differences.
$4$ is the number of years, not the factor.
A factor of $100$ is two labeled steps, from $A$ to $C$; $B$ is one step above $A$.

items.q: The line's slope is measured in powers of $10$ per year: the change in $\log y$ divided by the change in $t$. What is the slope?

options: $\log y$ rises $2$ (two powers of $10$) in $8$ years.
That is $\frac{2{,}000 - 20}{8}$, the slope on an ordinary scale; this axis shows $\log y$.
$10$ is the factor over $4$ years, not the change in $\log y$ per year.
That is $10^{0.25}$, the growth factor $b$; the slope is its logarithm, $0.25$.

items.q: Model the data with $y = a \cdot b^t$. Find the yearly growth factor $b$, correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the slope, which is $\log b$. Then $b = 10^{0.25}$.
That spreads the factor of $10$ evenly as $\frac{10}{4}$; the factor per year is the fourth root, $10^{1/4}$.

why.correct: $\log b$ is the slope, $0.25$, so $b = 10^{0.25} \approx 1.778$. Check: $1.778^4 \approx 10$, the factor over $4$ years.

items.q: Use the model $y = 20 \cdot 10^{t/4}$ to estimate the number of users at $t = 6$ years, correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is halfway between $200$ and $2{,}000$ in value. On a log scale, halfway up is the geometric middle, $\sqrt{200 \cdot 2{,}000}$.

why.correct: $y = 20 \cdot 10^{6/4} = 20 \cdot 10^{1.5} \approx 632.456$ users. On the plot, that point is halfway between $B$ and $C$ in height, but not in value.

options: $y$ is exponential in $t$
$y$ is linear in $t$
$y$ is logarithmic in $t$
$y$ is quadratic in $t$

why.correct: $\log y$ increases by $0.3$ for each step of $1$ in $t$, so $\log y$ is linear in $t$ and $y$ is exponential.
options: $\log y$ linear in $t$ means $y = a \cdot b^t$.
It is $\log y$, not $y$, that grows by equal amounts.
A logarithmic $y$ would make $y$ itself change by equal steps over equal factors of $t$.
$\log y$ has constant first differences, so it is linear, and $y$ is exponential.

items.q: Write $\log y$ as a linear function of $t$.

mistakes.why: The intercept is the value at $t = 0$, $0.5$; the slope is the change per step, $0.3$.
The slope is the change, $0.8 - 0.5 = 0.3$, not the second value.

why.correct: The starting value at $t = 0$ is $0.5$ and the constant change is $0.3$ per unit of $t$: $\log y = 0.5 + 0.3t$.

items.q: Which equation gives $y$ as a function of $t$?

options: Undo the logarithm with base $10$, then split the exponent.
That is $\log y$, not $y$.
The intercept and slope are logarithms of $a$ and $b$, so $a = 10^{0.5}$ and $b = 10^{0.3}$.
$10^{0.5 + 0.3t}$ is a product of powers, not a sum.
$0.5$ is $\log y$, not $y$.
That multiplies instead of using a power: $y = 10^{0.5}$.
The scale is base $10$, so undo $\log$ with $10$, not $e$.

items.q: By what factor is $y$ multiplied each time $t$ increases by $1$? Give the exact value.

mistakes.why: $0.3$ is the change in $\log y$. The factor is $10^{0.3}$.
Adding $0.3$ to a logarithm multiplies by $10^{0.3}$, not by $1.3$.

why.correct: Each step adds $0.3$ to $\log y$, which multiplies $y$ by $10^{0.3}$ (about $2$).

items.q: Which function's graph is a straight line on a semi-log plot (logarithmic vertical axis)?
options: $y = 5 \cdot 3^x$
$y = 5 + 3\log x$
An exponential function becomes linear when you take its logarithm.
$\log(5x + 3)$ is not linear in $x$; the graph bends.
$\log(x^3) = 3\log x$, which is not linear in $x$.
$\log(5 + 3\log x)$ is not linear in $x$.

items.q: A semi-log plot with a natural-log scale shows the line $\ln y = 1.2 + 0.05t$. Write $y$ as a function of $t$.

mistakes.why: That is $\ln y$. Raise $e$ to it to get $y$.
The intercept $1.2$ is $\ln a$, so $a = e^{1.2}$, not $1.2$.
$e^{1.2 + 0.05t}$ is a product, $e^{1.2} \cdot e^{0.05t}$, not a sum.

items.q: Why is the graph of $y = 3 \cdot 2^x + 10$ not a straight line on a semi-log plot?
options: Adding $10$ makes $\log y$ nonlinear in $x$
The base $2$ is too small for a semi-log plot
The coefficient $3$ bends the graph
Its outputs are negative for some $x$

why.correct: Only $y = a \cdot b^x$ has $\log y = \log a + x\log b$, a linear function. With a vertical shift, $\log(3 \cdot 2^x + 10)$ is not linear: the graph flattens toward $\log 10$ on the left.
options: The vertical shift breaks the product form that the logarithm turns into a line.
Any base $b > 0$, $b \ne 1$, gives a line when there is no shift.
A coefficient becomes $\log 3$, a vertical shift of the line, not a bend.
$3 \cdot 2^x + 10$ is always more than $10$, so its outputs are positive.

items.q: On a semi-log plot with a base-$10$ scale, the line through exponential data rises from $\log y = 1$ at $x = 0$ to $\log y = 3.5$ at $x = 5$. What is the growth factor $b$ in $y = a \cdot b^x$? Give the exact value.

mistakes.why: $0.5$ is the slope, which equals $\log b$. Then $b = 10^{0.5}$.
That is $a = 10^1$, from the intercept. $b$ comes from the slope.

items.q: Data that are exactly linear, such as $y = 4x + 2$ for $x \ge 0$, are plotted on a semi-log plot. What does the graph look like?
options: A curve that rises and is concave down
A straight line with positive slope
A curve that rises and is concave up
A horizontal line

why.correct: Equal additions of $4$ are smaller and smaller factors as $y$ grows ($2$ to $6$ triples, $6$ to $10$ is $\times 1.67$), so $\log y$ rises by shrinking steps.
options: Shrinking steps in $\log y$ over equal steps in $x$: concave down.
Only exponential data give a straight line.
The steps in $\log y$ shrink, so the curve bends down.
$y$ increases, so $\log y$ does too.

items.q: Exponential data $y = a \cdot b^x$ with $a > 0$ and $b > 1$ are drawn on a semi-log plot. Predict the effect of each change.

variables.name: The slope of the line, when $b$ increases
variables.why: The slope is $\log b$, which grows with $b$.

variables.name: The slope of the line, when $a$ increases
variables.why: $a$ only moves the line up, since $\log y = \log a + x\log b$.

why.correct: On a semi-log plot, $\log y = \log a + x\log b$: $a$ sets the intercept and $b$ sets the slope.

items.q: Two exponential models are drawn on one semi-log plot. Line $P$ is steeper than line $Q$. What does that tell you?
options: $P$ has the larger growth factor
$P$ has the larger starting value
$P$ is linear and $Q$ is exponential
$P$ gives the larger output for each $x$ value

why.correct: The slope of each line is $\log b$, so the steeper line has the larger $b$. Starting values come from the intercepts.
options: Slope $= \log b$, larger for larger $b$.
The starting value $a$ sets the intercept, not the steepness.
Both are straight on a semi-log plot, so both are exponential.
If $Q$ starts much higher, it can stay above $P$ for a while.
